do_more: Start with a concise, curiosity‑driven hook (question or bold statement) in the first 3‑5 seconds
Keep the script tight ~30 seconds, focusing on one clear takeaway
Use plain language without emojis; let the quote or lesson speak for itself
Frame titles as a direct promise or challenge, e.g., “You can turn over a new leaf every hour”
Repeat a single key phrase or visual cue to aid binge‑watching
avoid: Long, emoji‑filled titles that try to cram multiple ideas
Overly broad or generic summaries that lack a specific hook
short.title_style: Use a short, punchy statement or question that promises an immediate insight or action, without emojis.
next_tests: Produce two versions of the same short: one 30 s (tight) and one 42 s (standard) to compare VPD
Add a direct question hook versus a statement hook and measure impact
Create titles with and without the word “shorts” to see click‑through effect
short.best_title: You can turn over a new leaf every hour if you choose

do_more: Frame titles as direct, provocative questions targeting the viewer's personal certainty ("Question what you know", "How sure are you that you are right").
Focus on timeless philosophical frameworks and practical dilemmas rather than broad historical author biographies.
Keep titles punchy and under 10 words to maximize curiosity gap.
Lead the first 5 seconds of the script with an immediate existential or cognitive challenge.
avoid: Using documentary-style titles that sound like book reports ("The Essay That Changed American Thinking").
Relying solely on famous book titles and author names as the primary hook.
Making titles overly academic or descriptive.
full.title_style: Winning titles use direct second-person confrontation and philosophical interrogation rather than historical book summaries.
